json.summary: A junk-collector truck driver finds a groaning man lying on his load of old mattresses and pillows. The man says the driver ran him over last Tuesday on Gubacs Teréz út and broke both his legs. The driver blusters and denies it, and wonders how the man didn't starve in a week. The man says the accident happened as he left the shop, with two big bags. The driver curses his luck and groans. Then, with the same gruff "bazme" attitude, he hands the man a blanket because the nights are getting cold. The joke is the dry reversal. The driver acts annoyed and innocent but has clearly kept the victim on his truck for a week, and he ends up caring for him like a piece of cargo. The phone-number sign, "I'll pick up", adds a pun on picking up junk and picking up a person.

characters.name: truck driver
characters.description: Middle-aged, stocky, unshaven man with a curly comb-over, a vest with many pockets and a sleepy, grumpy face. He drives a junk-removal truck. He speaks in rough, gruff working-class Budapest slang, swears mildly to strongly ("mi a faszom", "gecit", "a kurva élet") and keeps adding the filler "bazme" (from "baszd meg"). He is defensive and denies guilt, but is secretly caring.

characters.name: injured man on the truck
characters.description: Off-panel voice from the truck bed. He lies hidden in the pile of mattresses and pillows and is never shown. He has two broken legs and speaks in deadpan, matter-of-fact tones. He tells his story with exact place names and gives mundane details, like the shopping bags, without drama. He groans ("HRAHGHHRRR", "AAAARRRGH").

panels.description: The driver hops or stumbles beside his truck, which is piled high with bedding. He holds a small object, apparently keys or a lighter. A broom sticks up from the load. The side of the truck says "ÉPÖIPAI KITTELEZÉS • OG". The scribbled "HLOTT!" and "RITY!" look like sound or action lettering.

The load on the truck groans from a bubble whose tail goes down into the stack. The driver stands to the right with hands on hips, looking startled and annoyed, and says "Mi a faszom?". The sign on the truck gives the phone number.

The driver, in profile, asks who is in his truck. His tail runs down to his own head. The injured man's bubble on the left sits over the load, with the line "FEKSZEM ITT." next to it. The phone number is on the truck.

The driver leans one arm on the load and frowns. His tail goes down to his head and he says he wasn't there. The man's bubble (r9) points to the load and begins the story of last Tuesday. The phone number is on the truck.

The driver shakes his fist and is skeptical. The bubble above him is his, with the tail running down to him. The bubble on the left, with the tail pointing to the truck load, belongs to the injured man, who explains what happened with the bags.
The driver walks off scratching his head and curses "A kurva élet!". The truck stands on the left with the same number.
Only the truck is shown. The injured man groans from a bubble above the load. The phone number is on the truck.
The driver, with an outstretched hand, offers or throws a blanket (the bedding on the load) and says it is cold at night. The truck on the left shows a pile of pillows and the phone number sign.

notes: Punchline: the driver blusters that he has nothing to do with it, yet in the last panel he gives the man a blanket. He has apparently been carrying a man with two broken legs on his truck for a week. The gag is the callousness mixed with gruff care.

"Bazme" (r4, r8, r21) is a vulgar filler, short for "baszd meg" (literally "fuck it"). It is used like "damn" or "for fuck's sake". It is a verbal tic of the driver. Keep it coarse and casual. It appears in r4, r8 and r21.

"Mi a faszom?" (r2) literally means "what the dick". It is a crude "what the fuck?". "Mi a gecit keresel" (r4) literally means "what the (vulgar) are you doing/looking for". The tone is rude and aggressive. "A kurva élet" (r15) literally means "the whore life" and is a very common curse meaning "fucking hell". "Ne kamuzz" (r12) means "don't bullshit/lie" ("kamu" is slang for fake).

The injured man says "Gubacs Teréz úton ütöttél el" (r5). The name is an invented or odd street. It is a mix of Gubacsi út (a real Budapest road) and Teréz (körút). Keep a fake-sounding local street name. "FEKSZEM ITT" (r6) means "I'm lying here" and is written as a sign-like line from the man.
"Fáj. Fájogat." (r5) means "It hurts. It keeps hurting". The repetition with the diminutive verb is a deadpan understatement from a man with two broken legs.

The signs "7722.683/FELVESZEM" (r3, r7, r11, r14, r16, r20, r22) are a phone number plus "felveszem", which means "I'll pick it up/answer". It is a junk-pickup advertisement. The sign stays the same in every panel, with small handwriting differences, so there is no scrambling gag. Keep the number as drawn and translate "felveszem", with a hint at the double meaning pick up/answer. The pun on picking up junk and people is the point.

The truck sign in p0, "ÉPÖIPAI KITTELEZÉS • OG" (r0), is garbled lettering, probably a mangled house-clearing slogan. Keep it as drawn or approximate it. The "HLOTT!" and "RITY!" are outside the editable boxes. "HLOTT" resembles "hullott" (fallen). Do not translate them unless needed.

The driver's "Hogy nem haltál éhen?" (r12) means "How come you didn't starve?". The weak excuse of the man (r13), that he was hit while carrying shopping bags, is both a plot detail and an absurd explanation. "Szatyor" means a plastic or cloth shopping bag, a typical Hungarian everyday word.
The register is rude, colloquial speech, mostly in capitals. The spelling "JÁRTAM" for "jártam" is just regular lettering. "Telibe kapott" means "hit me squarely" and is colloquial.
"Plédet" (r21) is a blanket/throw. Saying "nights are already cold" is the gruff driver's weak excuse for kindness.
